content.statement: setTimeout(fn, 0) runs fn immediately, before the rest of the current synchronous code.

remember: A zero-delay timer still waits until the call stack is empty and all microtasks have run.

content.prompt: A script calls setTimeout(fn, 0), then starts a promise chain in which every .then callback schedules another .then callback, forever. What happens to fn?

options.text: fn never runs, because the microtask queue never empties
fn runs first, because it was scheduled before the promises
fn runs once its delay has passed, between two promise callbacks
fn runs after a fixed number of microtasks, when the runtime yields

remember: The microtask queue drains completely, including newly added microtasks, before the next timer can run.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: A timer scheduled from a microtask still queues behind timers that were scheduled earlier.

content.prompt: A script calls setTimeout(T1, 0), then Promise.resolve().then(P1), then logs "end". T1 schedules Promise.resolve().then(P2). P1 schedules setTimeout(T2, 0). In what order do these run?

remember: After every macrotask the microtask queue drains, so P2 runs right after T1 and before T2.

content.statement: Calling resolve a second time with a new value replaces the value of an already fulfilled promise.

remember: A promise settles only once; later resolve or reject calls are ignored.

content.prompt: You call Promise.all([a, b, c]) and b rejects while a and c are still pending. What happens?

options.text: It rejects with b's error right away; a and c keep running
It waits for a and c, then rejects with an array of all errors
It resolves with the values of a and c, and undefined for b
It rejects with b's error and cancels a and c

remember: Promise.all rejects on the first rejection and cancels nothing; use Promise.allSettled to wait for every result.

content.prompt: A script runs three lines in a row: Promise.resolve().then(a1).then(a2); Promise.resolve().then(b1).then(b2); setTimeout(t, 0). All callbacks are plain synchronous functions. In what order do they run?

remember: Each .then is queued only when the step before it settles, so two chains interleave one step at a time.

content.prompt: "all saved" is logged and the connection is closed before the inserts finish. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Mark the first then callback as async

remember: Inside a then callback, return the promise you start; otherwise the chain moves on without waiting for it.

content.statement: An async function always returns a promise, even when its body returns a plain value like 42.

remember: async wraps the return value in a promise, so callers must await it or use then.

content.prompt: fetchUser() and fetchOrders() each take about 1 second and do not depend on each other. About how long until load() resolves?

options.text: About 1 second: the two awaits run in parallel
About 1 second: async functions run on a worker thread
Immediately: await does not block the thread
About 2 seconds: fetchOrders waits for fetchUser

remember: Sequential awaits run one after another; start independent work first and await Promise.all to run it in parallel.

content.prompt: checkStock(cart) is async and resolves to true or false. Orders are created even when items are out of stock. Find the bug.

remember: A promise object is always truthy; await it to get the value it resolves to.

content.prompt: What does this print?

options.text: b1 a1 end a2 b2 p
b1 end a1 a2 p b2
b1 a1 end a2 p b2
b1 a1 end p a2 b2

remember: An async function runs synchronously up to its first await; its caller resumes only in a later microtask, after the awaited call settles.

content.statement: A function returned from another function can still read and update the outer function's local variables after the outer function has returned.

remember: Closures keep outer variables alive; they capture the variable itself, not a snapshot of its value.

content.prompt: What is a closure?

options.text: A function that is called immediately after it is defined
A function bundled with the scope it was created in
A function that cannot access variables outside its own body
An object whose fields are hidden with the # prefix

remember: A closure is a function plus the scope it was created in; that is how inner functions keep their outer variables.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: Each call to the outer function creates a fresh scope, so every returned closure has its own count.

content.prompt: Each counter should keep its own value, so the last line should log 0. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Reset count = 0 as the first line of makeCounter
Use regular methods instead of arrow functions

remember: Closures share the variable they capture; to give each object its own state, declare it inside the factory.

content.statement: Inside an arrow function, this is the object the arrow function was called on.

remember: Arrow functions have no this of their own; they use this from the scope where they were written.

content.prompt: What happens on the last line?

options.text: It returns "Hi, " with an empty name

remember: Calling a method without its object loses this; in strict mode this is undefined. Use bind or an arrow wrapper.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so seconds goes up by one every second.

remember: Passing this.tick hands over the function without its object; wrap it in an arrow function or bind it.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: An arrow class field keeps this from construction; a detached method loses it, and class code is always strict.
With ==, null and undefined are equal to each other and to nothing else.

content.prompt: How do you reliably check whether x is NaN?

remember: NaN is not equal to anything, including itself; test for it with Number.isNaN.

content.prompt: Three of these comparisons evaluate to true. Which one evaluates to false?

remember: === never converts types; == converts both sides, usually to numbers, before comparing.

content.prompt: Match each comparison with how it treats types, NaN and -0.

right.text: No conversion; NaN equals NaN; 0 equals -0
No conversion; NaN equals NaN; 0 differs from -0
No conversion; NaN never equals NaN; 0 equals -0

remember: Object.is is === without the NaN and -0 exceptions; includes only fixes NaN.

content.statement: If a function calls push on an array it received as an argument, the caller's array changes too.

remember: Arrays and objects are passed as references; changing them inside a function changes the caller's value.

content.prompt: Which copy lets you change copy.user.name without changing state.user.name?

remember: Spread and Object.assign copy one level, so nested objects stay shared; structuredClone makes a deep copy.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: Assigning an array to another variable copies the reference, not the array.

content.prompt: withDefaults should fill in missing options without changing the object it receives, but userOpts ends up with retries. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Freeze the input first with Object.freeze(options)
Declare result with let instead of const

remember: Assigning an object to a new variable does not copy it; spread it first if you plan to change it.

content.statement: A function declaration can be called on a line above the place where it is written, in the same scope.

remember: Function declarations are hoisted together with their body, so they can be called before their line.

content.prompt: What does this log?

remember: var declarations are hoisted and start as undefined; only the assignment stays on its line.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: A function declaration is hoisted with its body; a function expression stored in a var is hoisted as undefined.

content.prompt: Each snippet runs on its own at the top level of a script. Three of them throw a ReferenceError. Which one runs without an error?

items.text: const g = () => z; g(); let z = 1;
const f = () => y; let y = 1; f();

remember: The temporal dead zone is about time, not position: a function may read a later let if it runs after that line.

content.statement: A variable declared with let inside an if block can still be used after the block ends.

remember: let and const are block-scoped: they exist only between the braces where they are declared.

content.prompt: Which statement about var is true?

options.text: var cannot be declared twice in the same scope
Using a var before its line throws a ReferenceError
var is scoped to the function, not to the block

remember: var belongs to the whole function; a var declared in a loop or an if is visible in the entire function.

content.prompt: This should log 30, but it throws a TypeError. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Use let instead of const for p
Move the total declaration inside the loop

remember: const forbids reassignment, and += is a reassignment; use let for values that change.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the loop logs every number and i does not exist after the loop.

remember: let gives the loop counter block scope; const cannot be incremented and var leaks out of the loop.
Without a compare function, sort compares values as strings; pass (a, b) => a - b to sort numbers.

content.prompt: Which of these methods changes the array it is called on?

remember: splice edits the array in place; slice, map and filter return new arrays.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the code logs 16.

remember: Give reduce an initial value of the type you are building, such as 0 for a sum.

content.prompt: Match each array method with what it does to the array and what it returns.

right.text: Does not mutate; returns a copy of a portion

remember: push, splice and sort change the array in place; slice leaves it alone and returns a new array.
The empty string is the only falsy string; "0" and "false" are truthy.

content.prompt: What are the values of "5" + 3 and "5" - 3?

remember: + concatenates as soon as one side is a string; -, * and / always convert to numbers.

content.prompt: Three of these expressions evaluate to "object". Which one does not?

remember: typeof gives "object" for null, arrays and dates; only functions get their own "function" result.

content.prompt: Match each expression with its result.

remember: + runs left to right and switches to concatenation once it meets a string; * always converts to numbers.

content.statement: A try/catch catches an error thrown inside a setTimeout callback that was scheduled inside the try block.

remember: A timer callback runs later on a fresh call stack, after the try block has finished, so that try/catch never sees it.

content.prompt: In current versions of Node.js, what happens by default when a promise rejects and no handler is ever attached to it?

options.text: Nothing; the rejection is silently ignored
The process crashes with an unhandled rejection error
The error is caught by the nearest try/catch on the call stack
The process logs a warning and keeps running

remember: Since Node.js 15 an unhandled rejection crashes the process; always await a promise or attach a catch.

content.prompt: Inside an async function, const res = await fetch(url) sits in a try block, and the request fails. Put the steps in order.

steps.text: The catch block runs with the error
The function pauses at await and other code can run
The rejection is thrown at the await line

remember: await turns a rejection into a throw at the await line, which is what lets try/catch handle it.

content.prompt: When the request fails, the page should fall back to a Guest profile, but the error reaches the top level instead. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Change it to: return await fetchProfile(id);

remember: Inside try, return await: a promise returned without await settles after the try has ended, so catch never runs.
